phonemes.desc: Written ym in Ugaritic cuneiform; conventionally vocalised “Yammu”. The word means “sea”.
The Canaanite sea-god, rival and enemy of Baʿal, defeated in the great Baal Cycle of Ugarit.
The name needs no vowels the Ugaritic scribes would not have recognised — a plain transliteration.

pronunciation.note: He is the sea itself as god: the oldest named enemy in the Baal Cycle, defeated at the world’s beginning.

domains.title: The Sea, Rival of Baʿal
domains.subtitle: The Defeated God of the Ugaritic Tablets
domains.lead: Yammu is the Canaanite sea-god: the personified ocean whose rebellion against the divine council set the Baal Cycle in motion, and whose defeat by Baʿal — with two magic clubs thrown from the storm-cloud — established the storm-god’s kingship over the gods. The Ugaritic tablets of the fourteenth century BCE, found in 1929, gave him back his name after three thousand years of silence.

cards.name: The Sea Itself
cards.desc: His name IS the word “sea” (ym) — the ocean as the first rebel against order.

cards.name: The Two Clubs
cards.desc: “Chaser” and “Driver”, the magic clubs Baʿal threw to shatter his skull — the cycle’s most quoted scene.

cards.name: The Divine Council
cards.desc: He demanded Baʿal’s surrender from the council of El; the gods’ cowardice set the war in motion.

cards.name: The Tablet’s Return
cards.desc: Found at Ugarit (Ras Shamra) in 1929 — the Baal Cycle restored Canaanite religion to history.

mythology.lead: Yammu’s mythology is the Baal Cycle’s opening act: the sea demands the storm-god’s surrender, the council wavers, and Baʿal — armed by the craftsman-god Kothar-wa-Khasis with two magic clubs — goes out to meet the flood and splits the sea’s skull between the eyes. It is the Levant’s own dragon-combat — the same pattern as Marduk and Tiamat, Indra and Vritra, told in the oldest alphabetic literature on earth.

myths.title: The Embassy of the Sea
myths.text: The cycle opens with Yammu’s envoys at the divine council, demanding that Baʿal be delivered into the sea’s power. El, the aged king of the gods, wavers — and it is left to Baʿal himself, with Kothar-wa-Khasis’s weapons, to answer the demand. The scene sets the cycle’s whole theology: kingship is taken, not granted.

myths.title: The Two Magic Clubs
myths.text: Kothar-wa-Khasis gives Baʿal two clubs — Yaggarish, “Chaser”, and Ayyamarri, “Driver”. Baʿal strikes Yammu between the eyes, on the skull: ‘Yammu is dead! Baʿal is king!’ The lines are the Levantine storm-god’s coronation — and the pattern that Hebrew poetry would echo in its own sea-combat, Yahweh versus Yam.

myths.title: Yam in the Psalms
myths.text: The Hebrew Bible keeps the sea-god’s name as a common noun and his defeat as a motif: ‘Thou didst divide the sea (yam) by thy strength’, ‘thou rulest the raging of the sea (yam)’. The Ugaritic tablets revealed what the Psalms were arguing against — and what they preserved: Yammu’s defeat is the Old Testament sea’s backstory.

myths.title: The Sea-Enemy Pattern
myths.text: Yammu belongs to the oldest myth-complex in the lexicon: the storm-god versus the sea. Tiamat and Marduk in Babylon, Vritra and Indra in the Rigveda, Typhon and Zeus in Greece — the pattern crosses the whole ancient world, and the Ugaritic telling is among its most vivid witnesses. The sea is always first, and always beaten.

lore.syncretism: Yammu is the Canaanite branch of the ancient Near Eastern sea-enemy — Tiamat’s cousin, with the Babylonian goddess-dragon as his nearest kin. The Hebrew tradition suppressed him into a noun but kept his combat; and modern study of the Baal Cycle restored him as the indispensable witness to what Israel’s religion argued with. The Greeks of the coast heard Poseidon in him; the scholars hear the pattern.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Baal Cycle’s discovery in 1929 rewrote the history of Canaanite and biblical religion — Yammu’s defeat gave the Psalms their sea-imagery’s original. In Ugaritic studies his name heads every syllabus; and the sea-monster pattern he anchors remains the comparative mythologist’s oldest exhibit.
lore.extendedMeditation: Yammu: the sea’s own name, restored in plain letters that the fourteenth-century scribes would have recognised. He needs no vowel-marks the tablets did not carry — the plain transliteration IS the restoration, and the skull-split the literature remembers.

sources.name: KTU 1.2 (the Baal Cycle, tablets from Ras Shamra)

lore.archaeology: Yammu’s monuments are the tablets: the Baal Cycle’s cuneiform pages from Ras Shamrt (Ugarit), 1929 — the oldest large alphabetic texts ever found, and the foundation-stones of Northwest Semitic philology.
lore.cult: No surviving cult of Yammu — he was the defeated one, and defeated gods get no temples. But the Baal Cycle’s ritual setting suggests the combat was re-enacted; and the sea’s own liturgy, the storm on the coast, kept his name in the ear.
lore.iconography: No image of Yammu survives — the tablets describe, they do not draw. His icon is the divided sea of the Psalms: the waters standing like walls, the combat fossilized into weather.
lore.reception: Comparative religion’s sea-combat paradigm runs through him — the Ugaritic telling is the pattern’s Levantine anchor. Biblical studies uses his cycle to read the Psalms’ sea-imagery as polemic; and the history of writing counts his tablets among its most consequential finds.
